query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the composition of AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloys by increasing the content of oxide-forming elements (e.g., Ti and/or adjusting Al) will improve tribo-corrosion degradation resistance at elevated temperatures by promoting the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent, self-healing spinel oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline AlCoCrFeNi HEA with standard concentrations of oxide-forming elements.
generation.intervention: Tailor the alloy composition by increasing Ti (and/or adjusting Al) content to enhance oxide scale formation.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature environments under simultaneous mechanical wear and exposure to a corrosive, chloride-rich medium.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent nano-scale spinel (or related) oxide layer on the alloy surface during service.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced oxide-forming element content promotes rapid, in situ generation of a protective oxide scale during high-temperature tribological and corrosive exposure. This scale acts as a self-healing barrier that mitigates further substrate degradation by reducing wear and limiting corrosion progression.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in wear rate and mass loss due to tribo-corrosion degradation compared to conventional structural alloys or unoptimized AlCoCrFeNi HEAs.
generation.baseline: Conventional structural alloys or AlCoCrFeNi HEAs with standard oxide-former content that do not readily form continuous self-healing oxide layers under combined high temperature and tribo-corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness is expected only under conditions where the kinetics of oxide scale formation are favorable. Excessively high additions of oxide-formers may destabilize the microstructure, and in extremely aggressive corrosive conditions the protective scale may not form or adhere properly.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentrations of Ti and/or Al for achieving consistent, protective oxide scale formation under varied tribo-corrosive conditions remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA samples with incremental increases in Ti (and/or adjusted Al) content. Expose these samples to elevated temperatures while subjecting them to simultaneous mechanical wear in a chloride-rich corrosive environment. Use in situ X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to monitor oxide scale formation and adherence, while measuring wear rates and mass loss over time.
measurements: Mass loss across defined exposure periods
Microstructural analysis including oxide scale thickness and continuity
Adhesion strength of the formed oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the oxide-former content does not result in the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale or if there is no statistically significant reduction in wear rate and mass loss compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. decision.trend: Early HEA studies first focused on understanding phase stability, precipitation, and basic mechanical behavior. Soon thereafter, researchers began probing high‐temperature wear performance of AlCoCrFeNi‐based alloys – as in the work on AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 – where elevated temperature wear tests revealed that, under friction, the formation of nano‐scale oxide (spinel) phases can markedly reduce wear depth. Around the same time, related work on similar alloy systems demonstrated significantly improved corrosion resistance (e.g., reduced mass loss and shallower depletion fronts) compared with conventional alloys in aggressive high-temperature chloride environments. However, while both wear and corrosion have been investigated individually in these HEAs, the combined phenomenon of tribo‐corrosion degradation under coupled high temperature and mechanical wear conditions has not been addressed in a comprehensive, systematic way.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to design an alloy system that not only leverages the intrinsic corrosion resistance of HEAs but also actively forms a self‐healing, adherent protective oxide scale during simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack at high temperatures.
decision.lever: Optimize the composition of AlCoCrFeNi‐based HEAs by tailoring the relative amounts of oxide‐formers (for example, by controlled addition or adjustment of Ti and/or Al) to promote the in situ generation of a continuous, adherent spinel (or related) oxide scale during service.
decision.why: Because prior studies have shown that specific compositions (like those containing Ti additions) can trigger the formation of beneficial oxide phases that improve high-temperature wear and corrosion resistance separately, the next logical step is to adjust the alloy’s composition to deliberately enable self-healing surface oxide formation under the combined tribo-corrosion environment typical of extreme operating conditions.
